16.0.s.en: 1. Return to the second contrast: between the quail and the frogs

16.0.0.en: 1 Therefore they were worthily punished by the like, and tormented by a multitude of insects. 2 But thy people, instead of that punishment, thou didst treat graciously by preparing quails, meat of a strange taste, wherewith thou satisfiedst their desire. 3 So that, while those, with their hunger, lost all desire for food through loathing of what thou didst send upon them, these, after a short want, partook of meat of a strange taste. 4 For it was meet that upon those oppressors inevitable want should come, and that these should only see how their enemies were tormented.

16.0.1.en: Therefore they were justly punished by the like of these, and were tormented by a multitude of insects. [1]

16.0.2.en: We saw in chapter eleven (Wis 11:16-20) the contrast between the plague of the Egyptians by the frogs, the gnats, the flies and the locusts, and the gift of the quail to the believers in the wilderness. The ancient Egyptians worshipped some insects and animals, so they were struck by their very gods.

16.0.3.en: This is what the wise man affirms here: “They were justly punished by the like of these.” What befell them was the fruit of these acts of worship, and God wished them to discover the truth of these false gods.

16.0.4.en: What they thought to be the source of their happiness became the source of their torment. This is the nature of sin: it carries its poison within it. He who thinks that he is enjoying its pleasure drinks its poison without knowing it.

16.0.5.en: When Moses the prophet was enraged against the people of Israel because they had worshipped the golden calf, he “took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it” (Ex 32:20). Some ask: why did he make them drink of the water in which the powdered golden calf was? He wished to assure them that what they had done, they drink of. For he who commits sin tastes its bitterness, and discovers that its pleasures are temporary and passing, hiding behind them the bitterness of death.

16.0.6.en: * Moses ground up the calf and made them drink it in the water of testing, so that all who had lived to worship the calf died by drinking it.

16.0.7.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian St. Augustine sees that Moses the prophet ground up the calf and made the children of Israel drink so that they might be crushed by repentance for the sin they had committed. So God permitted the worshippers of the idols of insects to be disciplined by the plagues of insects, so that their life might be made bitter and they might be crushed and repent, and return to the true God.

16.0.8.en: But thy people thou didst not punish, but didst treat graciously:

16.1.0.en: So that, to satisfy their keen appetite, thou didst prepare for them meat of a strange taste, that is, the quail. [2]

16.1.1.en: The people murmured against God and His prophet Moses, and asked for flesh in the wilderness, so He sent them quail, a bird like the partridge, which came migrating until it was weary of flying, so that its course was near the surface of the sea, and when it set out toward the camp, the people caught it very easily. The Lord smote them with a very great plague (Num 11:33) because of their murmuring.

16.1.2.en: Here he does not mention the murmuring, nor the great plague that was for their discipline, but he mentions that God does not leave His believers in need or hunger, and that the people could have eaten and given thanks to God for His gift instead of continual murmuring. The hearts of the ancient Egyptians were bound to the idols as gods, so their bodies, their animals and their crops were struck. So they became afflicted and hungry, in great distress, although they were in the fertile land of Egypt. Whereas the hearts of the believers were bound to God, so they were satisfied with the manna that came down from heaven, and with the quail sent to them in the midst of the wilderness, even though those who murmured against God fell under discipline.

16.1.3.en: The psalmist says: “The people asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven” (Ps 105:40), and St. Augustine comments on this psalm that the people comprised two groups, one group that believed and trusted in God, and God was pleased with them, and another group that bore weariness and murmuring against God. The former ate and rejoiced, and the latter were smitten by God for their murmuring.

16.1.4.en: Here he speaks of those who trusted in God, whom the mixed multitude of the Egyptians did not drive to the lust for eating flesh (Num 11:4), nor did they remember with the rest of the people what they used to eat as slaves in Egypt, the (small) fish, and the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick (Num 11:5). These enjoyed the quail and the manna as delicious and wonderful food.

16.2.0.en: So that those, though hungry, lost all desire for food, because of the loathsomeness of what was sent upon them, while these, after a short want, shared meat of a wonderful taste. [3]

16.2.1.en: For the worshippers of idols in their hunger lost the desire for food, since their houses were filled with the stench of the dead frogs, and their bodies were struck by the bites of the gnats, their animals by boils, and their crops by the locusts. Everything became loathsome to them. But those who trusted in God enjoyed the wonderful food in the wilderness.

16.3.0.en: For it was meet that upon those oppressors inevitable want should come, and that these should see how their enemies were tormented. [4]

16.3.1.en: The portion of the unjust enslavers was not wealth, honor and authority, but want, that is, extreme poverty, hunger and need, a thing from which there is no escape, that is, there is no way to flee from it.

16.3.2.en: In contrast to this, while the believers enjoyed divine gifts in the wilderness, they remembered the plagues that had befallen their enslavers, and so they marveled at the work of God’s wisdom with them.

16.3.3.en: When the children of Israel saw what had befallen those who unjustly opposed them, they offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, who had kept them from these plagues and brought them out into the wilderness, where they practice praises and experience true joy and rest.

16.4.s.en: 2. The third contrast: the locusts and the bronze serpent

16.4.0.en: 5 For when the terrible fury of wild beasts came upon these, and they were destroyed by the bites of crooked serpents, 6 thy wrath endured not to the end, but they were troubled for a little season for a warning, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law, 7 for he that turned himself toward it was saved, not by that which he saw, but by thee, O Saviour of all. 8 And in this thou didst prove to our enemies that thou art he who delivereth from all evil, 9 for them the bitings of locusts and flies killed, neither was there found any remedy for their life, for they were worthy to be punished by such. 10 But thy sons not even the teeth of venomous dragons overcame, for thy mercy came and healed them. 11 For they were pricked that they should remember thy words, and were quickly saved, lest falling into deep forgetfulness they should be deprived of thy goodness. 12 For neither herb nor mollifying plaister restored them to health, but thy word, O Lord, which healeth all things. 13 For thou hast power of life and death: thou leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again. 14 A man indeed killeth through his malice, but he cannot bring the spirit again that is gone out, neither release the soul that is received.

16.4.1.en: Even when the dreadful fury of wild beasts came upon these, and the bites of the crooked serpents destroyed them, thy wrath endured not to the end. [5]

16.4.2.en: Without partiality, when the people fell into murmuring and returned in their hearts to the land of bondage, desiring the perishable food (Num 11:5), He gave them the desire of their hearts and sent them quail. They ate greedily and gluttonously and did not offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, so by their continual murmurings they made themselves worthy of the deadly serpents; but when they returned to Him, He removed the plague from them by setting up a bronze serpent, which is a type of the Cross.

16.4.3.en: It is written in the Book of Numbers: “And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread. And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died. Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned… And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole… And it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived” (Num 21:5-9). Those who returned to God in repentance through Moses found the bronze serpent, and so enjoyed new life.

16.5.0.en: But they were troubled for a little while for a warning, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law. [6]

16.5.1.en: Discipline by the fiery serpents was necessary, so that God might warn them, showing them how grave their situation was. But God commanded that the bronze serpent be set up as “a sign of salvation,” so that they might remember the divine Law, which presents to them prophecies and types of the salvation promised to Adam and his sons.

16.5.2.en: Thus God turned even their evils to good, so long as they seek to return to Him and to know His divine mysteries.

16.5.3.en: * Tell me, did not God command through Moses that no images or likenesses be made of anything in heaven or on earth? And yet did He not Himself ask Moses to make the bronze serpent in the wilderness? Moses made it as a sign by which those bitten by serpents are healed. In doing this, was not Moses free from any sin? In this, as I said before, God declared through Moses a mystery by which He breaks the power of the serpent that drove Adam to sin. He promises that He will save from the bites of the serpent (that is, from evil works, idolatry and other sins) all who believe in Him, who died by this sign, which is the Cross.

16.5.4.en: St. Justin Martyr * The serpent struck Adam in Paradise and killed him. And it also struck Israel in the camp and destroyed it.

16.5.5.en: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (Jn 3:14).

16.5.6.en: Just as those who looked with their bodily eyes at the sign that Moses fixed on the pole lived bodily, so also those who look with spiritual eyes at the body of the Messiah nailed and hung on the Cross and believe in Him shall live spiritually.

16.5.7.en: This was proclaimed through the bronze serpent, which by nature does not suffer, so that He who by nature cannot die might suffer on the Cross.

16.5.8.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * It is a great mystery, the healing from the serpent. What does it mean, healing from a serpent by looking at a serpent? It is healing from death by faith in one who is dead! Yet Moses was afraid and fled from the serpent (Ex 4:3). What does it mean that Moses fled from that serpent? What is this, brethren, but what we know was fulfilled in the Gospel? Christ died, and the disciples were afraid and withdrew from that hope in which they had been.

16.6.0.en: St. Augustine For he that turned himself toward it was saved, not by that which he saw, but by thee, O Saviour of all. [7]

16.6.1.en: Some may ask: how does the Lord Christ say, “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” (Jn 3:14)? Is the Lord Christ being likened to the serpent, or does the deadly serpent signify the Lord Christ, the giver of life? The answers of the Fathers of the Church came many and mutually harmonious:

16.6.2.en: First: the Lord Christ bore the sins of the world (Jn 1:29), so the Lord Christ took our place, and accepted to bear our death in order to raise us to His life. For in the Crucified we see what the Lord Christ bore on our behalf, the fruit of our sins, that He might kill it by His death.

16.6.3.en: Second: St. Augustine sees that the lifted-up serpent is dead, and it is a symbol of the death which the Lord Christ accepted by His own will in order to kill our death.

16.6.4.en: Third: St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that the children of Israel looked at the bronze serpent, dead and lifted up on a pole, and so perceived that by the Cross death died and became motionless!

16.6.5.en: Fourth: Origen has a marvelous comment concerning the Cross, for he sees in it two realities: the first is apparent, namely that Jesus Christ, in His love for mankind and His obedience to the Father, was lifted up on the Cross by His own will. The second is hidden, namely that the one who was crucified and lost his movement and authority is the devil, since the handwriting that was against us was nailed to the Cross, and principalities and powers were spoiled of their authority and were made a show of openly in a bitter defeat (Col 2:14-15). So the serpent that was lifted up represents, on the one hand, the Lord Christ who bears our sins, and on the other hand, the ancient serpent whom the Lord Christ nailed with His Cross and stripped of its authority over the believers.

16.7.0.en: * Perhaps you ask: for what purpose did Christ not say plainly, “I shall be crucified,” but directed his hearers to an ancient type (the serpent)? We say to you: first, that you may know that the sayings of the Old Testament agree with the New, and that those are not strange to these. Second: that you may know that Christ did not come into the world unwillingly. Besides these two reasons, that you may know that the Lord suffered no harm from the reality of these (sufferings), and that these sufferings, for many, proceed out of salvation. So that no one may say: how can those who believe in the Crucified be saved if death itself laid hold of Him? Therefore He leads us to the ancient story. For if the Jews by looking at a bronze image of the serpent escaped death, how much more shall those who believe in the Crucified enjoy, for good reason, greater benefits. For the crucifixion does not take place through the weakness of the Crucified, or because the Jews are stronger than He, but because “God so loved the world” [16], therefore His living temple (His body) hastened to the Cross.

16.7.1.en: St. John Chrysostom * What are the serpents that bite? The sins that proceed from the death of the body.

16.7.2.en: What is the serpent that was lifted up? The death of the Lord on the Cross. As death came by the serpent, it was symbolized by the image of a serpent.

16.7.3.en: The bite of the serpent is deadly, and the death of the Lord is life-giving. When one looks at a serpent, the serpent loses its power. What is this? When one looks at death, death loses its power. But whose death? The death of Life…

16.7.4.en: By the death of Christ (the Life) death died.

16.7.5.en: The death of Life slew death, the fullness of life swallowed up death.

16.7.6.en: Death was dissolved in the body of Christ.

16.7.7.en: Therefore we say at the Resurrection, as the victors sing: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (1 Cor 15:54)…

16.7.8.en: There is a difference between the symbolic image and the real thing: the symbol gives temporary life, and the reality of which it is the symbol gives eternal life.

16.7.9.en: * To present a type of His Cross, Moses, at the command of the merciful God, lifted up the image of a serpent on a pole in the wilderness, in the likeness of the sinful flesh which had to be crucified in Christ, who was typified (Jn 3:14). It was to look at this Cross that the psalmist purposed when he said: “Mine eyes fail for thy salvation, and for the word of thy righteousness” (Ps 119:123), because He made Christ Himself “sin for us, in the likeness of sinful flesh, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (Rom 8:3; 2 Cor 5:21).

16.7.10.en: For the sake of declaring the righteousness of God he says that his eyes have failed from looking with zeal and fervor, while he remembers human weakness, looking to the divine grace in Christ.

16.7.11.en: St. Augustine * That bronze serpent was hung up as a remedy for the bites of serpents, not as a type of Him who suffered, but of the opposite. It healed those who looked at it, not because they believed that it lived, but because it was slain, and with it was slain the one subject to it, for it deserves to perish. And what inscription suitable to it shall we inscribe? “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (Hos 13:14; 1 Cor 15:55). You have been cast down by the Cross. You have no longer a soul; you have died motionless, though you retain the form of a serpent raised on a pole!

16.7.12.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus And in this thou didst prove to our enemies that thou art he who delivereth from all evil. [8]

16.7.13.en: For those the bitings of locusts and vermin killed, and no remedy was found to preserve their life, for they were worthy to be punished by such. [9]

16.7.14.en: By the ten plagues God did not display His power, for He is not in need of human glory, but He showed His people their possibilities, in that they enjoy the power of God through their faith. And at the same time He showed the weakness of the gods of the Egyptians, unable to protect them even from the locusts or the gnats (flies).

16.7.15.en: * “He spake, and the locusts came, and caterpillers, and that without number, and did eat up all the herbs in their land, and devoured the fruit of their ground” (Ps 105:34-35). The trees were destroyed by the hail and the fire, and the gardens and the crops by the locusts and the caterpillers (the young locusts before they have wings), for it wasted not only the fruit but even the plant itself.

16.7.16.en: Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus Whereas the teeth of venomous serpents did not overcome thy sons, for thy mercy came upon them and healed them. [10]

16.7.17.en: The wise man stands in amazement before two scenes: an unbelieving people struck with insects and perishing, because they did not believe in the Physician who heals souls; and a believing people struck with venomous serpents and healed, because they believed in the Savior who gives victory over the powers of darkness.

16.7.18.en: If feeble insects cause destruction while the fangs of venomous serpents do not prevail over the believers, this is not a natural matter; rather, healing is accomplished according to the riches of God’s grace, His surpassing mercy and His wonderful salvation. This is the mystery of the Cross!

16.7.19.en: Concerning the bronze serpent, it is not the serpent that gives healing, but “thy mercy came and healed them” (Wis 16:10).

16.7.20.en: For they were pricked that they should remember thy words, and were quickly delivered, lest falling into deep forgetfulness they should neglect thy goodness. [11]

16.7.21.en: The Lord commanded Moses the prophet to lift up the dead bronze serpent on a pole, so that when the believers look at it they may remember God’s promises of salvation. He hastened and healed them, lest they fall into the depth of forgetfulness and lose their hope in the promised salvation.

16.7.22.en: And neither herb nor ointment healed them, but thy word, O Lord, for it healeth all. [12]

16.7.23.en: He did not give them medicinal herb or ointments for healing, not to prevent them from using medicines, but lest they ascribe their healing from the bites of the serpent to medicines and not to the word of God and His promise of salvation.

16.7.24.en: St. Basil the Great presented to us in his “Long Rules,” question number 55, a long and engaging discourse on the Christian view of medicine and physicians, and on whether it is permissible to have recourse to the art of medicine and to use medicines while keeping the practice of godliness. I translated it, arranged it and published it in the book “What do the Fathers say about sickness?” I quote a little of it here.

16.7.25.en: * All the arts (crafts) are a gift to us from God, remedying the deficiencies of nature. So He gave us agriculture, because the harvest which the earth gives us without cultivation is not sufficient for our needs. And the craft of weaving, because the use of clothing is necessary for modesty and for protection from the wind. In the same way as regards the craft of building, and so also as regards the craft of medicine. For since our body is exposed to various pains, some attacking from outside, and others from within because of the food we eat, and since the body suffers from surfeit as well as from lack of food, therefore the art of medicine is granted by God, who directs all our life, as a pattern for the healing of the soul, to lead us to remove what is superfluous and to obtain what is lacking.

16.7.26.en: * We would not have needed the toil of the farmer if we were living in the delights of Paradise; so also we would not have sought the art of medicine for healing if we were immune from sickness.

16.7.27.en: So it was at the time of creation before the fall, as a gift from God. But after we were driven out of that place, and heard the words: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Gen 3:19), then with toil and exhausting hardship we established the craft of agriculture to remove the misery that followed the curse that had come. And God gave us the knowledge and understanding for this craft, when we returned to the earth from which we were taken and were bound to a body full of pains, and were cast into the judgment of corruption because of sin.

16.7.28.en: For the same reason we became subject to sickness, and God gave us the craft of medicine for the treatment of the sick, even if only to a certain degree.

16.7.29.en: * The herbs that are used for the treatment of every sickness did not grow in the earth spontaneously, but it is clear that it is the will of God that they should grow from the soil to serve our needs. Our enjoyment of the natural benefits latent in the roots of herbs, their flowers, leaves, fruits and juice, and even in some minerals and products of the sea, is necessary for bodily health, and they are regarded like food and drink.

16.7.30.en: St. Basil the Great * The art of medicine is not a hindrance to godliness, but you must practice it with the fear of the Lord.

16.7.31.en: Father Barsanuphius By saying: “it healeth all,” he makes clear that if a certain people benefited by bodily healing from the deadly serpents by looking at the bronze serpent, then it is a type of the Cross, which offers salvation to the whole world. “God so loved the world, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (Jn 3:16).

16.7.32.en: For thou hast power of life and death: thou leadest down to the gates of hell, and bringest up from it. [13]

16.7.33.en: As the wise man looks at the One hung on the Cross, he sees Him not only as the Physician who can heal all men, but as the Almighty, the giver of life and resurrection, and the Judge who carries His believers to eternal glory while the gates of Gehenna are opened before the unbelievers, since they chose of their own will to withdraw from the giver of life. God breathes into us the spirit of power and victory, so that neither the devil nor death has authority over us. “Thou leadest down to the gates of the realm of the dead, and bringest up from it.”

16.7.34.en: A man can kill by his wickedness, but he cannot bring back the breath that has gone out, nor set free the soul that is held fast! [14]

16.7.35.en: Man by his free will delivered himself over to death by sin, but he is unable to recover the lost Paradise or true life; but God alone can raise the dead, bodily or spiritually, and restore man to something greater than he was in the garden of Eden.

16.7.36.en: If a man thinks that he has authority to kill by his wickedness and injustice, does he have authority to bring the slain back to life?

16.8.s.en: 3. The fourth contrast: the hail and the manna

16.8.0.en: 15 For it is not possible for any one to escape thy hand, 16 for the ungodly, who denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thine arm, and were pursued with strange waters, hail and rains, and consumed with fire. 17 And what is most strange, the fire was more intense in the water, which quencheth all things, for the world fighteth for the righteous. 18 For sometime the flame was mitigated, that it might not burn up the living creatures sent against the ungodly, but that they might see and perceive that God’s judgment pursued them; 19 and sometime it burneth even in the midst of water above the power of fire, that it might destroy the fruits of an unrighteous land. 20 Instead of which things thou feddest thine own people with angels’ food, and didst send them from heaven bread prepared without their labour, able to content every man’s delight, and agreeing to every taste. 21 For thy substance declared thy sweetness unto thy children, and serving to the appetite of him that took it, tempered itself to every man’s liking. 22 The snow and ice endured the fire, and melted not, that they might know that fire burning in the hail and sparkling in the rain destroyed the fruits of the enemies. 23 But this, again, forgot its own strength, that the righteous might be nourished. 24 For the creature that serveth thee, who art the maker, is made more intense for the punishment of the unrighteous, and is relaxed for the benefit of such as put their trust in thee. 25 Therefore even then was it altered into all fashions, and was obedient to thy grace, that nourisheth all things, according to the desire of them that had need, 26 that thy children, O Lord, whom thou lovedst, might know, that it is not the growing of fruits that nourisheth man, but that thy word preserveth them that put their trust in thee. 27 For that which was not destroyed of the fire, being warmed with a little sunbeam, melted away, 28 that it might be known that we must prevent the sun to give thee thanks, and at the dayspring pray unto thee. 29 For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter’s hoar frost, and shall run away as unneedful water.

16.8.1.en: It is impossible to escape from thy hand. [15]

16.8.2.en: Often man in his pride thinks that he is able to lord it over his brother, to oppress and persecute, and that there is no law that can restrain him. These were the feelings of Pharaoh and his counselors and men, as they mocked and humbled the Hebrews. These did not perceive that God is the Almighty, and that “it is impossible to escape from his hand.”

16.8.3.en: Pharaoh made the plan firm to destroy Moses and the people of God: the sea before them, the army behind them, and the mountains on both sides, while they had no weapons, no military experience and no fortresses in which to take refuge. But God made for His people a way of salvation in the midst of the sea, and that very way became the total destruction of Pharaoh.

16.9.0.en: For the wicked, who denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thine arm, pursued by unusual rains, and hailstones, and harsh tempests, and consumed by fire. [16]

16.9.1.en: Pharaoh defied God Himself, for in a spirit of domination and violence he said to Moses that he did not know the Lord, but only knew his own authority and material gains, without any regard for God, the Creator of all, or for showing kindness to his brethren in humanity.

16.9.2.en: God let nature itself answer the wicked Pharaoh. Egypt does not know hail, and yet, contrary to nature, He disciplined the pagan Egyptians with hail. And what is astonishing is that hail and fire (lightning) do not occur together, but the two opposites worked together by divine permission for discipline…

16.9.3.en: By this nature stopped the mouth of the arrogant Pharaoh, to declare to him that he had lost all reason and wisdom, by resisting the wisdom of God.

16.10.0.en: And what is most strange, in the water which quencheth all things, the fire grew more intense, for the universe fighteth for the righteous. [17]

16.10.1.en: Water is used to extinguish fires, but what happened to Pharaoh was that whenever the hail fell the flames grew more intense, so the two opposites agreed together to discipline him.

16.11.0.en: And the flame was sometimes quieted, lest it should burn up the animals that were sent against the wicked, but that they might see and understand that a divine judgment pursued them. [18]

16.11.1.en: The wise man stood in amazement, for the natural phenomena that rose up in an unnatural manner against the unbelieving pagans worked together. Note that the fires did not burn the insects and animals sent for their discipline, as though everything had joined together against the unbelievers to drive them to faith.

16.11.2.en: The unnatural factors removed from the wicked any possibility of imagining that what was happening was by chance; rather, they came to carry out a divine judgment against them for their discipline.

16.12.0.en: And sometimes it burneth even in the midst of water above the power of fire, that it might destroy the produce of an unjust land. [19]

16.12.1.en: When fires break out, especially in an agricultural land, people’s dream becomes the falling of rain able to put out the fires. But what happened was that in the midst of the hail the fires grew more intense in their flaming, and the losses increased.

16.12.2.en: * “He gave them hail for rain, and flaming fire in their land. He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts” (Ps 105:32-33)… The clouds changed their natural role, and sent hail instead of rain, thunderbolts and whirlwinds accompanied by hail, and water and fire. Although by nature the one is contrary to the other, no confusion occurred between them. The fire did not melt the frozen water or the hail, nor did the fire put out the flame. Besides their leaving the natural resistance of each to the other, they brought a severe punishment on the Egyptians, to condemn their enslavement and their disrespect for their nature (as human beings). For though they were men, they oppressed their fellows in humanity with cruel bondage. Therefore even their vines and their fig trees and all kinds of plants were utterly destroyed by the fire and the hail.

16.13.0.en: Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus But thy people, instead of this, thou didst feed with angels’ food, and didst present to them from heaven bread prepared, which they did not labour for, bread that supplied every delight and suited every taste. [20]

16.13.1.en: While nature rose up against the wicked and did not keep to the natural factors, so also, contrary to the laws of nature, it worked on behalf of the believers, offering them manna from heaven, a thing of which mankind had never heard before.

16.13.2.en: The manna is considered the food of angels (Ps 78:25; 105:40), because it points to the heavenly sweetness that each person tastes according to what he desires.

16.13.3.en: * “Each one tasted the manna in his mouth according as he longed” (cf. Wis 16:20)… In any case, this can be realized for the believers and not for those who murmur against God, those who certainly would not seek other food, since the manna gave them a taste according to what they wished.

16.14.0.en: St. Augustine For thy substance declared thy sweetness unto thy children, and satisfying the desire of him that took it, was changed to what every man would. [21]

16.14.1.en: There is a rabbinic tradition that the manna had a special flavor which each person experienced according to what he desired, so that each person found in it a sweet taste suited to his wish.

16.14.2.en: * Would then that we hasten to receive the heavenly manna. This manna grants a taste to every mouth according to what it desires. Hear also the Lord saying to those who approach Him: “As thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee” (Mt 8:13). So also if you receive the word of God which is preached in the Church with perfect and devout faith, the word becomes for you according to what you desire. For example, if you are sad, it comforts you, saying to you: “A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:19). If you are exulting in your coming hope, it lavishes joys upon you, saying: “Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye righteous” (Ps 32:11). If you are in anger, it gives you calm, saying: “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath” (Ps 37:8). If you are in pain, it heals you, saying: “The Lord healeth all thy diseases” (cf. Ps 103:3). If you are consumed by poverty, it comforts you, saying: “The Lord raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the needy out of the dunghill” (cf. Ps 113:7). So the manna of the word of God gives a taste to your mouth according to what you wish.

16.14.3.en: Origen Here we stand in wonder before God’s indulgence of His believers, for not only does He give them what is for their satisfaction, growth and progress, but He gratifies every believer, giving him what he desires so long as it is for his good and benefit.

16.14.4.en: When the believer is in the bosom of God, and feels that he is carried on the everlasting arms, everything becomes sweet in his throat, it satisfies his needs, and he lacks nothing at all.

16.15.0.en: The snow and ice endured fire and melted not, that it might be known that the fruits of the enemies were consumed by fire blazing in the hail and flashing in the midst of the rains. [22]

16.15.1.en: A marvelous picture of God’s surpassing love for man, for He moves nature even against its laws to serve man, so He permits the fire to blaze in the midst of the hail and the heavy rains. Man is the object of God’s care, so He lays out a plan for him and gives him a message, and turns all things to his good if he loves God (Rom 8:28).

16.16.0.en: Whereas this fire forgot even its own power, that the righteous might be nourished. [23]

16.16.1.en: As though nature, in its longing to serve man, the object of God’s love and care, is ready to disregard its characteristics and forget its properties, to work for the benefit of the righteous believers, even contrary to its laws.

16.17.0.en: For the creation, which serveth thee who art its maker, is strained for the punishment of the unjust, and is relaxed for the benefit of those who trust in thee. [24]

16.17.1.en: Nature does not work blindly according to its laws; rather, while keeping the natural laws, which are the work of God, it moves and reacts according to the Creator’s plan, so it works for the benefit of the righteous believers of the Lord, and is harsh upon the unbelievers for their discipline, to the extent that the Creator permits.

16.17.2.en: The fire that could not melt the manna when the believers cooked it in the wilderness did not hurt the insects and animals sent to discipline the pagan Egyptians during the plagues. The fire that did not burn the three holy youths in Babylon is the one that killed the soldiers who cast the youths into it, and is the one that harmed the Egyptians and their crops and their plantings during the plagues.

16.18.0.en: Therefore then it was changed into every form, and was in the service of thy gift that nourisheth all, according to the desire of those who had need of it. [25]

16.18.1.en: In His wisdom God created man to govern the world with righteousness and holiness, for when he is bound to his Creator, God moves nature to work in his service according to what he asks and desires.

16.19.0.en: So that thy sons whom thou lovedst, O Lord, might know that it is not the produce of the fruits that nourisheth man, but thy word preserveth those who trust in thee. [26]

16.19.1.en: The Holy Scripture is accustomed to call the believers the beloved of the Lord. They are the object of His love and care. Therefore what nature offers them is from the hand of God, according to His word or His divine promises.

16.20.0.en: For that which the fire did not destroy was melted away when warmed by a little sunbeam. [27]

16.20.1.en: The wise man marvels as he looks at the manna sent to them from God, for it does not endure the rays of the sun even in the early morning. If a man was late in his sleep he could not gather manna, for he would find it melted by the rays of the sun. And at the same time that he gathers the manna he cooks it, and the heat does not melt it nor spoil it, but it becomes fit for eating.

16.21.0.en: So that it might be known that we must rise before the sun to give thee thanks, and meet thee at the rising of the light. [28]

16.21.1.en: The wise man urges us to rise early to God, so that He may be the beginning in all the days of our life, and before every work He may have the first place in our hearts, and He pours out upon us the riches of His surpassing gifts. For he who does not hasten before sunrise cannot gather the manna, and remains hungry all his day; for God satisfies the soul with heavenly food when it rises early to Him.

16.21.2.en: * Concerning the place (of prayer): “I will therefore that men pray every where” (1 Tim 2:8). Concerning the direction (of prayer) it is written in the Wisdom of Solomon: “That it might be known that we must prevent the sun to give thee thanks, and meet thee at (before) the rising of the light” (Wis 16:28).

16.22.0.en: Origen For the hope of the ungrateful shall melt away like the winter frost, and shall run away like water that is of no use. [29]

16.22.1.en: The wise man sees in those who rose early to gather the manna before sunrise the class of those obedient to the divine commandment with thanksgiving to God, the maker of good things; and as for those who in negligence wait until the sun rises, like those who do not believe the divine words, they are ungrateful and deniers of kindness. The former find delicious food offered to them freely, which may be called “the bread of angels,” and the latter find the manna turned to water like frost in the cold of the wilderness, good for nothing, for it cannot be gathered for drinking nor does it water plants, because the wilderness is a desert.

16.22.2.en: * What greater thing does (the Lord) ask of us than that we ask Him that we may be thankful in return for this tender care of His? Let us then obey, and keep this in everything. For there is nothing that ruined the Jews like their ingratitude; plagues upon plagues befell them for no other reason than this. Indeed, over and above these plagues, their souls perished and were corrupted. “For the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter’s hoar frost” (Wis 16:29). For it paralyzes the soul and kills it as happens with bodies.

16.22.4.en: Who satisfies me but you, O Wisdom of God?

16.22.5.en: * With the greatness of the gifts and abilities of my fathers the Pharaohs, they bowed down to idols of animals and insects, and so they drank of the very cup which they had filled.

16.22.6.en: They tasted bitterness from the plagues of the frogs, the gnats, the flies and the locusts.

16.22.7.en: Their houses were turned into tombs full of stench.

16.22.8.en: Their bodies found no rest, but pains and torment.

16.22.9.en: And their life became full of uncleanness; their crops the locusts ate, so they found no food for themselves.

16.22.10.en: * Grant me to cleave to You in the midst of the wilderness of this world.

16.22.11.en: I do not ask for bread or flesh; You are my satisfaction and my feast!

16.22.12.en: You are my joy and the exultation of my heart!

16.22.13.en: * My soul groans, because You grant me every fullness, while I see many of my brethren in humanity deprived and in ruin!

16.22.14.en: * Who heals me but You, O Physician of souls and bodies?

16.22.15.en: The unbelievers could not endure the plagues of feeble insects.

16.22.16.en: They perished because of the gnats and the flies, and went hungry because of the locusts.

16.22.17.en: But the believers, the bites of the deadly serpents could not destroy them.

16.22.18.en: They looked at the bronze serpent and were healed.

16.22.19.en: Let me look at Your Cross, and perceive that the powers of darkness have been stripped of their authority.

16.22.20.en: Death died, and it became impossible for it to move.

16.22.21.en: The bites of the deadly serpents were turned into a living witness to Your mercy.

16.22.22.en: You are the wonderful Physician of my soul.

16.22.23.en: You are the heavenly, saving medicine!

16.22.24.en: Who heals me but You, O Savior of the world?

16.22.25.en: * O the riches of Your wisdom and Your love for me!

16.22.26.en: For my sake You created nature with all its laws, seen and hidden.

16.22.27.en: You prepared it for my service, for I am Your beloved, and the object of Your care.

16.22.28.en: And for my sake also You permit its laws to be broken, at one time to satisfy my needs, and at another to discipline me.

16.22.29.en: All Your works are love and surpassing care.

16.22.30.en: By fire coming down from heaven to burn Sodom and Gomorrah, so that the believers may learn purity and fear uncleanness and abominations.

16.22.31.en: And You permitted the fire to become dew, so that the three holy youths might walk in it.

16.22.32.en: * How marvelous! When the fires fell upon the Egyptians for their discipline, they longed for rains to fall to put them out.

16.22.33.en: So rains fell, and even hail, but they did not put out the fires; rather they made them blaze the more.

16.22.34.en: * The fire could not melt the hail that fell upon the wicked, nor spoil the manna which the believers gather to cook.

16.22.35.en: It was not possible for the manna to endure the heat of the rays of the sun in the early morning, while it endured the blazing fires for its cooking.

16.22.36.en: * What shall I render to You, O my Creator?

16.22.37.en: For You move everything for my edification!

16.22.38.en: To You be glory, O You who are rich in love!
